stem: A learner needs the diameter of a thin copper wire, about $0.5\ \text{mm}$ across, as precisely as possible. Which instrument should she use?

options.content: A metre rule
options.rationale: A metre rule reads only to the nearest millimetre, which is bigger than the whole diameter.

options.content: A tape measure
options.rationale: A tape measure is for long distances and reads to about a millimetre.

options.content: Vernier callipers
options.rationale: Vernier callipers read to $0.1\ \text{mm}$: better than a rule, but not the most precise choice.

options.content: A micrometer screw gauge
options.rationale: Correct: a micrometer reads to $0.01\ \text{mm}$, ideal for a thin wire.

explanation: A micrometer screw gauge reads to $0.01\ \text{mm}$, so it gives the diameter of a thin wire most precisely.

stem: How should the volume of water in a measuring cylinder be read?

options.content: From the top of the curved surface, looking down
options.rationale: Looking down causes parallax, and for water the reading is taken at the bottom of the curve.

options.content: From the bottom of the meniscus, with the eye level with it
options.rationale: Correct.

options.content: From the side of the cylinder where the water touches the glass
options.rationale: The water creeps up the glass at the edges, so this reading is too high.

options.content: From the bottom of the meniscus, looking up from below
options.rationale: Looking from below causes a parallax error.

explanation: Read the bottom of the meniscus with your eye level with it to avoid parallax error.

stem: A stack of 25 identical metal washers is $38\ \text{mm}$ tall. What is the thickness of one washer?
workedSolution:
1. Thickness of one washer $= \dfrac{\text{height of stack}}{\text{number of washers}}$.
2. $= \dfrac{38}{25} = 1.52\ \text{mm}$.
hints: Divide the total height by the number of washers.

stem: A pendulum makes 25 complete oscillations in $51.0\ \text{s}$. Calculate its period.
hints: The period is the time for ONE oscillation.

stem: A hand-operated stop-watch that displays hundredths of a second measures the time of one swing of a pendulum to within 0.01 s.

answerSpec.feedbackFalse: Right: the person's reaction time, about 0.2 to 0.3 s at each end, is far larger than the display's 0.01 s.

explanation: Human reaction time (about 0.2 s to 0.3 s) limits a hand-operated stop-watch, whatever its display shows. Timing many swings and dividing reduces this error.

stem: Why do learners time 20 oscillations of a pendulum instead of just one?

options.content: The pendulum swings faster after many oscillations.
options.rationale: The period stays the same; that is why timing many works.

options.content: It reduces the effect of reaction-time errors on the value of the period.
options.rationale: Correct: the same reaction-time error is shared over 20 oscillations.

options.content: A stop-watch cannot measure a time as short as one second.
options.rationale: It can display it, but reaction time makes a single reading unreliable.

options.content: It removes the need to repeat the experiment.
options.rationale: Repeating and averaging is still good practice.

explanation: The reaction-time error at the start and end is the same whether you time 1 or 20 oscillations, so dividing by 20 makes it 20 times smaller per oscillation.

stem: On a pair of Vernier callipers the Vernier zero lies just past $2.3\ \text{cm}$ on the main scale, and the 7th Vernier division lines up exactly with a main-scale mark. What is the reading?
explanation: Main scale $2.3\ \text{cm}$ plus Vernier $7 \times 0.01\ \text{cm} = 0.07\ \text{cm}$, so the reading is $2.37\ \text{cm}$.
workedSolution: 1. Main scale $2.3\ \text{cm}$ plus Vernier $7 \times 0.01\ \text{cm} = 0.07\ \text{cm}$, so the reading is $2.37\ \text{cm}$.
hints: Each Vernier division adds 0.1 mm = 0.01 cm.

stem: A micrometer screw gauge reads $0.03\ \text{mm}$ when its jaws are closed with nothing between them. When a ball bearing is placed between the jaws, the sleeve shows $7.0\ \text{mm}$ and the thimble reads 36.

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: What is the reading on the micrometer with the ball bearing in place?

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: What is the name of the $0.03\ \text{mm}$ reading with the jaws closed?

options.content: A parallax error
options.rationale: Parallax comes from the angle of viewing.

options.content: A zero error
options.rationale: Correct.

options.content: A reaction-time error
options.rationale: That affects timing.

options.content: A random error
options.rationale: This error is the same every time, so it is systematic.

parts.explanation: A reading when the true value is zero is a zero error.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Calculate the true diameter of the ball bearing.

explanation: Reading $= 7.0 + 0.36 = 7.36\ \text{mm}$; the instrument already reads $0.03\ \text{mm}$ at zero, so the true diameter is $7.33\ \text{mm}$.
hints: A positive zero error must be subtracted.

explanation: $1\ \text{litre} = 1000\ \text{cm}^3$, and a millilitre is one thousandth of a litre, so $1\ \text{ml} = 1\ \text{cm}^3$.

stem: Match each measurement with the most suitable instrument.

left.content: The length of a laboratory bench
The volume of 40 ml of water
The time for 10 swings of a pendulum
The temperature of a cup of tea

explanation: Each instrument measures one quantity: length (rule), volume of a liquid (measuring cylinder), time (stop-watch), mass (balance), temperature (thermometer).

stem: What name is given to the error caused by reading a scale with your eye not directly in line with the mark?
explanation: Viewing a scale from an angle makes the pointer or liquid level appear against the wrong mark: a parallax error.

stem: A learner times 10 oscillations of a pendulum three times: $15.2\ \text{s}$, $15.6\ \text{s}$ and $15.4\ \text{s}$. Calculate the period of the pendulum.
workedSolution:
1. Mean of the three readings $= \dfrac{46.2}{3} = 15.4\ \text{s}$.
2. Period $= \dfrac{15.4\ \text{s}}{10} = 1.54\ \text{s}$.
hints: Then divide by the number of oscillations in each reading.

stem: When timing a swinging pendulum, why is it best to start and stop the watch as the bob passes the centre of its swing?

options.content: The bob is moving fastest there, so the moment it passes is easiest to judge.
options.rationale: Correct.

options.content: The bob stops there for a moment.
options.rationale: The bob is momentarily at rest at the ends of the swing, not the centre.

options.content: The period is shorter at the centre.
options.rationale: The period does not depend on where you time from.

options.content: It makes the pendulum swing for longer.
options.rationale: Where you time from has no effect on the pendulum.

explanation: At the centre the bob moves fastest, so the instant it passes a fixed marker is sharp. At the ends it slows and lingers, making the turning point hard to judge.

stem: A learner wants to find the thickness of one sheet of paper in a book whose pages are numbered 1 to 300. Each sheet carries two page numbers. She has a $30\ \text{cm}$ ruler marked in millimetres.

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Describe how she should measure the thickness of one sheet as accurately as possible with the ruler.

points.description: Squeezes the pages of the book together (excluding the covers) and measures the thickness of the whole block of pages with the ruler
Counts the number of sheets: 300 pages make 150 sheets
Divides the thickness of the block by the number of sheets (repeating and averaging if possible)

parts.explanation: Measure many sheets together, count the sheets (not pages), and divide.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: The block of pages is $1.8\ \text{cm}$ thick. Calculate the thickness of one sheet in millimetres.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Why can she not measure one sheet directly with the ruler?

options.content: The ruler's smallest division (1 mm) is much larger than the thickness of one sheet.
options.rationale: Correct.

options.content: Paper is transparent.
options.rationale: This does not stop a measurement.

options.content: The ruler has a zero error.
options.rationale: A zero error can be corrected; the problem is the precision.

options.content: A sheet is too long.
options.rationale: Its length is not the problem.

parts.explanation: One sheet is about a tenth of a millimetre thick, far smaller than the ruler's 1 mm divisions.

explanation: Measuring the block of 150 sheets ($18\ \text{mm}$) and dividing gives $0.12\ \text{mm}$ per sheet. A common trap is dividing by 300: pages are numbered on both sides of each sheet.
hints: How many sheets carry pages 1 to 300?

stem: Light gates connected to an electronic timer remove the reaction-time error of a hand-held stop-watch.
explanation: The timer starts and stops automatically when the object breaks the light beams, so no human reaction time is involved.
